'''''Pinus lambertiana''''' (commonly known as the '''sugar pine''') is the tallest and most massive [[pine]] tree and has among the longest [[Conifer cone|cones]] of any [[conifer]]. It is native to coastal and inland mountain areas along the [[Pacific coast]] of [[North America]], as far north as [[Oregon]] and as far south as [[Baja California]] in Mexico.

==Description==

=== Growth ===
The sugar pine is the tallest and largest ''Pinus'' species, commonly growing to {{convert|40|–|60|m|ft|round=5|sp=us}} tall, exceptionally to {{cvt|82|m|ft}} tall, with a trunk diameter of {{cvt|1.2|-|2.5|m|ftin}}, exceptionally {{cvt|3.5|m|ftin}}.<ref name="Arno">{{Cite book|last1=Arno|first1=Stephen F.|title=Northwest Trees: Identifying & Understanding the Region's Native Trees|last2=Hammerly|first2=Ramona P.|publisher=[[Mountaineers Books]]|year=2020|isbn=978-1-68051-329-5|edition=field guide|location=Seattle|pages=26, 30–35|language=en|oclc=1141235469|orig-date=1977}}</ref> The tallest recorded specimen is {{convert|83.45|m|ftin|abbr=on}} tall, is located in [[Yosemite National Park]], and was discovered in 2015.<ref>{{cite news | title = 3 Sierra sugar pines added to list of 6 biggest in world | newspaper = Associated Press | location = South Lake Tahoe, California | language = English | date = 31 Jan 2021| url = https://apnews.com/article/nevada-forests-south-lake-tahoe-17501dc8cb094fc7ffb1543426631bc6 | access-date = 13 Feb 2023}}</ref> The second tallest recorded was "Yosemite Giant", an {{cvt|82.05|m|ftin}} tall specimen in Yosemite National Park, which died from a [[bark beetle]] attack in 2007. Yosemite National Park also has the third tallest, measured to {{cvt|80.5|m|ftin}} tall as of June 2013; the [[Rim Fire]] affected this specimen, but it survived. The next tallest known living specimens grow in southern [[Oregon]]; one in Umpqua National Forest is {{cvt|77.7|m|ftin}} tall and another in Siskiyou National Forest is {{cvt|77.2|m|ftin}} tall. 
[[File:Pinus lambertiana ProspectOR.jpg|thumb|left|upright|Old sugar pines in the [[Rogue River – Siskiyou National Forest]], southern Oregon]]

The bark of ''Pinus lambertiana'' ranges from brown to purple in color and is {{Convert|5-10|cm|sp=us|frac=2}} thick.<ref name="Arno" /> The upper branches can reach out over {{Convert|8|m|abbr=on}}.<ref name="Arno" /> Like all members of the [[white pine]] group (''Pinus'' subgenus ''Strobus''), the [[leaves]] ("needles") grow in [[fascicle (botany)|fascicles]] ("bundles") of five<ref name="Arno" /> with a [[deciduous]] sheath. They are {{cvt|5|–|11|cm|in|frac=4}} long.<ref>{{Jepson eFlora|38280|Pinus lambertiana}}</ref> Sugar pine is notable for having among the longest [[conifer cone|cones]] of any conifer, mostly {{cvt|10|–|50|cm|in|0}} long,<ref name="Arno" /><ref name="FNA">{{eFloras|1|233500939|Pinus lambertiana |family=Pinaceae |first=Robert |last=Kral}}</ref> although they can occasionally reach as much as {{cvt|56|cm|in|0}}.<ref name="u078">{{cite web | title=Oregon State University | website=Landscape Plants | url=https://landscapeplants.oregonstate.edu/plants/pinus-lambertiana | access-date=2025-09-20}}</ref><ref name="FEIS">{{cite web |last=Habeck |first=R. J. | title=Pinus lambertiana | website=US Forest Service | date=1990-10-26 | url=https://www.fs.usda.gov/database/feis/plants/tree/pinlam/all.html | access-date=2025-09-20}}</ref> Although the cones of the [[Coulter pine]] are more massive; the unripe weight of {{Convert|1-2|kg}} makes the sugar pine's cones perilous projectiles when chewed off by squirrels.<ref name="Arno" /> The [[seed]]s are {{cvt|1|–|2|cm|in|frac=4}} long, with a {{convert|2|–|3|cm|in|frac=4|adj=on|abbr=off|sp=us}} long wing<ref name="FNA" /> that aids their dispersal by wind. Sugar pine never grows in pure stands, always in a mixed forest, and is [[shade tolerant]] in its youth.<ref>{{Gymnosperm Database |family=Pinaceae |genus=Pinus |species=lambertiana}}</ref>

=== Distribution ===
The sugar pine occurs in Oregon and [[California]] in the [[Western United States]] southward to [[Baja California]], specifically in the [[Cascade Range]], [[Sierra Nevada (U.S.)|Sierra Nevada]], [[Pacific Coast Ranges|Coast Ranges]], and [[Sierra San Pedro Martir]]. It is generally more abundant towards the south and can be found between {{Convert|500 and 1500|m|abbr=on}} above sea level.<ref name="Arno" />

===Genome===
The massive 31 gigabase mega-genome of sugar pine has been sequenced in 2016 by the large PineRefSeq consortium.<ref name=Stevens>{{cite journal|last=Stevens|first=K.A.|display-authors=et al.|date=2016|title=Sequence of the Sugar Pine Megagenome |journal=Genetics |volume=204|issue=4|pages=1613–1626|doi=10.1534/genetics.116.193227|pmid=27794028|pmc=5161289}}</ref> This makes the genome one of the largest sequenced and assembled so far.<ref name=Stevens/>

The transposable elements that make up the megagenome are linked to the evolutionary change of the sugar pine. The sugar pine contains extended regions of [[non-coding DNA]], most of which is derived from [[transposable element]]s. The genome of the sugar pine represents one extreme in all plants, with a stable diploid genome that is expanded by the proliferation of transposable elements, in contrast to the frequent polyploidization events in [[angiosperm]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gonzalez-Ibeas |first=Daniel |display-authors=et al.|date=2016 |title=Assessing the Gene Content of the Megagenome: Sugar Pine (''Pinus lambertiana'') |journal=G3 (Bethesda) |volume=6 |issue=12 |pages=3787–3802|doi=10.1534/g3.116.032805 |pmid=27799338 |pmc=5144951 }}</ref>

[[File:Sugarpine.jpg|thumb|right|Almost ripe female cones]]

=== Embryonal growth ===
In late stage of [[embryo]]nal development, the sugar pine embryo changes from a smooth and narrow [[paraboloid]] to a less symmetric structure. This configuration is caused by a transverse orientation of division planes in the upper portion of the embryo axis. The root initial zone is established, and the [[epicotyl]] develops as an anlage flanked by regions of that define the cotyledonary buttresses. At this stage, the embryo is composed of the [[suspensor]], root initials and [[root cap]] region, [[hypocotyl]]-shoot axis, and the [[epicotyl]]. The upper (distal) portion of the embryo, which gives rise to the [[cotyledon]]s and the epicotyl, is considered to be the [[shoot apex]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Berlyn |first=Graeme P |date=1967 |title=The Structure of Germination in Pinus Lambertiana Dougl. |journal=Yale School of Forestry & Environmental Studies, Bulletin Series |volume=77}}</ref>

=== Shoot apex ===
The [[shoot apex]] has the following four zones:<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sacher |first=J.A. |date=1954 |title=Structure and Seasonal Activity of the Shoot Apices of Pinus Lambertiana and Pinus ponderosa. |journal=American Journal of Botany |volume=41 |issue=9 |pages=749–759|doi=10.1002/j.1537-2197.1954.tb14406.x |bibcode=1954AmJB...41..749S }}</ref>
#The apical initials produce all cells of the shoot apex through cell division. It is located at the top of the [[meristem]] and the cells are larger in size compared to other cells on the surface layer.
#The central mother cell generates the rib meristem and the inner layers of the peripheral tissue zone through cell division. It presents a typical [[gymnosperm]] appearance and is characterized by cell expansion and unusual [[mitosis]] that occurs in the central region. The rate of mitosis increases on its outer edge. 
#The peripheral tissue zone consists of two layers of cells that are characterized by dense cytoplasm and mitosis of high frequency.
#Lastly, the rib meristem is a regular arrangement of vertical files of cells which mature into the pith of the axis.

==Etymology==
Naturalist [[John Muir]] considered sugar pine to be the "king of the conifers". The common name comes from the sweet resin, which [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Native Americans]] used as a sweetener.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.oregonencyclopedia.org/articles/sugar_pine/#.VZr15PmqpBc|title=Sugar pine|website=Oregonencyclopedia.org|access-date=18 June 2017}}</ref> John Muir found it preferable to [[maple sugar]].<ref name = Saunders>{{cite book |title=Edible and Useful Wild Plants of the United States and Canada |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4IwrWyK7OmQC&q=Edible+and+Useful+Wild+Plants+of+the+United+States+and+Canada |last=Saunders |first=Charles Francis |year=1976 |publisher=Courier Dover Publications |isbn=0-486-23310-3 |page=219 }}</ref> It is also known as the great sugar pine. The scientific name was assigned by [[David Douglas (botanist)|David Douglas]] in 1826,<ref name="Arno" /> in honor of the London botanist [[Aylmer Bourke Lambert]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Muir |first=John |title=The Mountains of California |date=2010 |publisher=Random House Publishing Group |others=Bill McKibben |isbn=978-0-375-75819-5 |series=Modern Library Classics Ser |location=Westminster |pages=112–114}}</ref>

==Ecology==
=== Wildlife ===
The large size and high nutritional value of the sugar pine seeds are appealing to many species. Yellow pine chipmunks (''[[Neotamias amoenus]]'') and Steller's jays (''[[Cyanocitta stelleri]]'') gather and hoard sugar pine seeds. Chipmunks gather wind-dispersed seeds from the ground and store them in large amounts. Jays collect seeds by pecking the cones with their beaks and catching the seeds as they fall out. Although wind is a main dispersal agent of sugar pine seeds, animals tend to collect and store them before the wind can blow them far.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Thayer |first1=T |last2=Vander Wall |first2=S |year=2005 |title=Interactions between Steller's jays and yellow pine chipmunks over scatter-hoarded sugar pine seeds |journal=Journal of Animal Ecology |volume=74 |issue=2 |pages=365–374 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2656.2005.00932.x |jstor=3505625 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2005JAnEc..74..365T }}</ref>

Black bears (''[[Ursus americanus]]'') feed on sugar pine seeds in the fall months within the Sierra Nevada. Both sugar pine and oak species are currently in decline, directly affecting black bear food sources within the Sierra Nevada.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mazur |first1=R |last2=Klimley |first2=AP |last3=Folger |first3=K |year=2013 |title=Implications of the variable availability of seasonal foods on the home ranges of black bears, ''Ursus americanus'', in the Sierra Nevada of California |journal=Animal Biotelemetry |volume=1 |issue=16 |page=16 |doi=10.1186/2050-3385-1-16 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2013AnBio...1...16M }}</ref>

=== Threats ===
The sugar pine has been severely affected by the white pine blister rust (''[[Cronartium ribicola]]''),<ref name="Moore2008">{{cite book |author1=Moore, Gerry |title=National Wildlife Federation Field Guide to Trees of North America |author2=Kershner, Bruce |author3=Craig Tufts |author4=Daniel Mathews |author5=Gil Nelson |author6=Spellenberg, Richard |author7=Thieret, John W. |author8=Terry Purinton |author9=Block, Andrew |publisher=Sterling |year=2008 |isbn=978-1-4027-3875-3 |location=New York |page=79}}</ref> a [[fungal pathogen]] accidentally introduced from Europe in 1909. A high proportion of sugar pines have been killed by the blister rust, particularly in the northern part of the species' range where blister rust has been present longer. The rust has also destroyed much of the Western white pine and [[whitebark pine]] throughout their ranges.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Maloney |first1=P |last2=Duriscoe |first2=D |last3=Smith |first3=D |last4=Burton |first4=D |last5=Davis |first5=D |last6=Pickett |first6=J |last7=Cousineau |first7=R |last8=Dunlap |first8=J |title=White Pine Blister Rust on High Elevation White Pines in California |url=http://www.caforestpestcouncil.org/2005%20CFPC%20Meeting/1506%20Maloney_Dunlap%2005BR%20Survey.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061009055647/http://www.caforestpestcouncil.org/2005%20CFPC%20Meeting/1506%20Maloney_Dunlap%2005BR%20Survey.pdf |archive-date=2006-10-09 |access-date=2007-02-05}}</ref> The [[U.S. Forest Service]] has a program for developing rust-resistant varieties of sugar pine and western white pine. Seedlings of these trees have been introduced into the wild. The Sugar Pine Foundation in the [[Lake Tahoe]] Basin has been successful in finding resistant sugar pine seed trees. Blister rust is much less common in California, where sugar, Western white and whitebark pines still survive in great numbers.<ref name="spf">{{cite web |title=Sugar Pine Foundation |url=http://www.sugarpinefoundation.org |access-date=18 June 2017 |website=Sugarpinefoundation.org}}</ref>

Sugar pine trees have been affected by the mountain pine beetle (''[[Dendroctonus ponderosae]]''), which is native to western North America. The beetles lay their eggs inside of the tree and inhibit the tree's ability to defend itself against invading species. Beetle infestation can also cause nutrient deficiencies that slowly weaken the tree's overall health, making pines more susceptible to other threats such as fires and [[white pine blister rust]].<ref>{{cite web |year=2012 |title=Mountain pine beetle |url=http://www.invadingspecies.com/mountain-pine-beetle/ |url-status=live |work=Ontarios invading species awareness program |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200927011833/http://www.invadingspecies.com/mountain-pine-beetle/ |archive-date=2020-09-27}}</ref> Blister rust can weaken the tree and enable further infestation by mountain pine beetles.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Van Mantgem |first1=PJ |last2=Stephenson |first2=NL |last3=Keifer |first3=M |last4=Keeley |first4=J |year=2004 |title=Effects of an introduced pathogen and fire exclusion on the demography of sugar pine |journal=Ecological Applications |volume=14 |issue=5 |pages=1590–1602 |doi=10.1890/03-5109 |jstor=4493673|bibcode=2004EcoAp..14.1590V }}</ref>

[[File:Cronartium ribicola Pinus lambertiana (03).jpg|thumb|upright|Sugar pine starting to succumb to white pine blister rust]]

The species is generally [[Fire ecology|resistant to fire]] because of its thick bark and because it clears away competing species.<ref name="Arno" /> However, its mortality has been directly linked to drier conditions and higher temperatures. Climate change presents a threat to species health: higher temperatures can decrease [[resin]] levels within the trees, weakening defenses against pathogens. At the same time, warmer winters increase survival of pests and pathogens. The weakened or dying trees then provide fuel for forest fires, which may become more frequent and more intense with rising summer temperatures, particularly if coupled with drier conditions and stronger winds.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Slack |first1=A |last2=Kane |first2=J |last3=Knapp |first3=E |last4=Sherriff |first4=R |year=2017 |title=Contrasting impacts of climate and competition on large sugar pine growth and defense in a fire-excluded forest of the central sierra nevada |journal=Forests |volume=8 |issue=7 |page=244 |doi=10.3390/f8070244 |doi-access=free|bibcode=2017Fore....8..244S }}</ref>

=== Protective efforts ===
Sugar pine trees are in slow decline due to several threats; white pine blister rust, mountain pine beetles, and climate change. Efforts to restore sugar pines and other white pine trees that have been impacted by invasive species, climate change, and fires have been undertaken by governmental and non-governmental entities. One nonprofit, the Sugar Pine Foundation, was created in 2004 to plant sugar pine seeds in the Sierra Nevada along the border of California and Nevada.<ref name="spf" /> They plant seedlings grown from seeds collected from tree strains resistant to blister rust. The foundation's aim is to build in the a wild a sugar pine population that is resistant to white pine rust.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Maloney |first1=PE |last2=Vogler |first2=DR |last3=Eckert |first3=AJ |last4=Jensen |first4=CE |last5=Neale |first5=DB |year=2011 |title=Population biology of sugar pine (''Pinus lambertiana'' Dougl.) with reference to historical disturbances in the Lake Tahoe Basin: Implications for restoration |journal=Forest Ecology and Management |volume=262 |issue=5 |pages=770–779 |doi=10.1016/j.foreco.2011.05.011|bibcode=2011ForEM.262..770M }}</ref>

==Uses==
[[File:Sugar Pine Bark.jpg|thumb|right|upright|Bark of a sugar pine on [[Mount San Antonio]] in the [[San Gabriel Mountains]] of Southern California]]

====Indigenous uses and traditions====
Indigenous peoples used several parts of the tree for food. The seeds were eaten raw or roasted, ground into flour, or pulverized into a paste, and the inner bark was also eaten.<ref name="Arno">{{Cite book|last1=Arno|first1=Stephen F.|title=Northwest Trees: Identifying & Understanding the Region's Native Trees|last2=Hammerly|first2=Ramona P.|publisher=[[Mountaineers Books]]|year=2020|isbn=978-1-68051-329-5|edition=field guide|location=Seattle|pages=26, 30–35|language=en|oclc=1141235469|orig-date=1977}}</ref> The sweet [[resin]] was consumed in small quantities and could also be chewed as gum.<ref name="Peattie">{{cite book |last=Peattie |first=Donald Culross |author-link=Donald C. Peattie |title=A Natural History of Western Trees |year=1953 |publisher=[[Bonanza Books]] |location=New York |page=55}}</ref><ref name="Arno"/> Its sweetness is largely attributed to the [[pinitol]] it contains.<ref name="Arno"/>

Sugar pine also had medicinal and ceremonial uses. Among the [[Washoe people|Washo]], ethnographer [[Robert H. Lowie]] recorded the use of a sugar pine preparation after childbirth.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Lowie |first=Robert H. |author-link=Robert H. Lowie |title=Ethnographic Notes on the Washo |journal=University of California Publications in American Archaeology and Ethnology |volume=36 |number=5 |year=1939 |pages=301–352 |url=https://digicoll.lib.berkeley.edu/record/82931/files/ucp036-006.pdf}}</ref> Among the [[Sierra Miwok]], eating the first sugar pine nuts of the harvest was preceded by pressing and blowing by a shaman, as with other first fruits.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Barrett |first1=Samuel A. |last2=Gifford |first2=Edward W. |title=Miwok Material Culture: Indian Life of the Yosemite Region |publisher=Board of Trustees of the Public Museum of the City of Milwaukee |year=1933 |series=Bulletin of the Public Museum of the City of Milwaukee |volume=2 |issue=4 |chapter=Conifers |url=https://www.yosemite.ca.us/library/miwok_material_culture/conifers.html}}</ref> In the [[Hupa]] Brush Dance, traditionally performed to cure a sick child, burning sugar pine pitchwood was waved over the child while a particular song was sung, and sugar pine bark was prepared as medicine.<ref>{{cite book |last=Keeling |first=Richard |title=Cry for Luck: Sacred Song and Speech Among the Yurok, Hupa, and Karok Indians of Northwestern California |publisher=University of California Press |year=1992 |pages=24–27 |url=https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/view?chunk.id=0&doc.view=print&docId=ft8g5008k8}}</ref>

Sugar pine also figures in traditional narratives. In the [[Achomawi]] [[creation myth]], Annikadel, the creator, makes one of the 'First People' by intentionally dropping a sugar pine seed in a place where it can grow. One of the descendants in this ancestry is Sugarpine-Cone man, who has a handsome son named Ahsoballache.<ref name="Woiche">{{cite book |title=Annikadel: The History of the Universe as Told by the Achumawi Indians of California |last=Woiche |first=Istet |editor1-last=Merriam |editor1-first=Clinton Hart |editor1-link=Clinton Hart Merriam |year=1992 |publisher=[[University of Arizona Press]] |location=[[Tucson, Arizona|Tucson]] |isbn=978-0-8165-1283-6 |oclc=631716557 }}</ref> After Ahsoballache marries the daughter of To'kis the [[Chipmunk]]-woman, his grandfather insists that the new couple have a child. To this end, the grandfather breaks open a scale from a sugar pine cone, and secretly instructs Ahsoballache to immerse the scale's contents in spring water, then hide them inside a covered basket. Ahsoballache performs the tasks that night; at the next dawn, he and his wife discover the infant [[Edechewe]] near their bed.<ref name="Woiche" /> <ref>{{cite book |title=Annikadel: The History of the Universe as Told by the Achumawi Indians of California |last=Woiche |first=Istet |editor1-last=Merriam |editor1-first=Clinton Hart |editor1-link=Clinton Hart Merriam |year=1992 |publisher=[[University of Arizona Press]] |location=[[Tucson, Arizona|Tucson]] |isbn=978-0-8165-1283-6 |oclc=631716557}}</ref> 

In a [[Wintu]] narrative recorded by [[Jeremiah Curtin]], a basket of sugar pine seeds is given to the people; although they eat from it, the basket remains full.<ref>{{cite book |last=Curtin |first=Jeremiah |author-link=Jeremiah Curtin |title=Creation Myths of Primitive America in Relation to the Religious History and Mental Development of Mankind |publisher=Little, Brown |year=1898 |page=206 |url=https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/39106/pg39106-images.html}}</ref>

====Timber====

Sugar pine was commercially logged in the [[Sierra Nevada]] during the [[California Gold Rush]], when local sawmills supplied lumber to mining districts and growing foothill communities.<ref>Heckendorn & Wilson, ''Miners & Business Men's Directory: for the Year Commencing January 1st, 1856'', Columbia, California, 1856.</ref> The tree was especially valued for its large, straight trunk, which could yield long lengths of clear lumber.<ref name="LarsenWoodbury1916">{{cite report |last1=Larsen |first1=Louis T. |last2=Woodbury |first2=T. D. |title=Sugar Pine |publisher=United States Department of Agriculture |series=Bulletin |number=426 |year=1916 |url=https://research.fs.usda.gov/sites/default/files/2023-03/psw-usda_bull426.pdf}}</ref> Its wood is lightweight, straight-grained, easily worked, and resistant to shrinkage and warping.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Kinloch |first1=Bohun B. Jr. |last2=Scheuner |first2=William H. |chapter=Sugar Pine |title=Silvics of North America |volume=1 |publisher=United States Department of Agriculture, Forest Service |year=1990 |pages=370–379 |url=https://research.fs.usda.gov/silvics/sugar-pine}}</ref> As supplies of [[eastern white pine]] declined in the early 20th century, sugar pine increasingly served as a western substitute.<ref name="LarsenWoodbury1916"/> In 1916, the [[United States Department of Agriculture]] described it as the most valuable commercial timber tree on the Pacific Coast and estimated that California contained about 39 billion board feet of standing sugar pine.<ref name="LarsenWoodbury1916"/>

[[File:Sugar Pine Lumber Company Mill Workers.jpg|thumb|Box-factory and planing-mill workers at the [[Sugar Pine Lumber Company]]'s [[Pinedale, California|Pinedale]] mill, where sugar pine was processed into finished lumber and wooden boxes, 1925.]]
Sugar pine lumber was used for building construction, boxes and crates, sash and doors, and millwork.<ref name="LarsenWoodbury1916"/> It also became important to California's fruit industry. Lumber cut in the Sierra Nevada was transported to mills and box factories in the [[San Joaquin Valley]], where its light weight and lack of taste or odor made it suitable for raisin trays and fruit boxes.<ref name="LarsenWoodbury1916"/> Clear, straight-grained sugar pine was also used for piano keys and [[organ pipe]]s.<ref name="Peattie"/><ref>"Buying Lumber for Keys". ''Music Trade Review'' 47:10 (5 September 1908), 35.</ref> The largest pipe of the [[Wanamaker Organ]] in Philadelphia, more than {{convert|32|ft|m}} long, is made of Oregon sugar pine.<ref>{{cite web |title=About the Organ |publisher=Friends of the Wanamaker Organ |url=https://wanamakerorgan.com/about-the-organ/ |access-date=September 4, 2026}}</ref> In 1902, two carloads of sugar pine from [[Madera County, California|Madera County]] were shipped to [[Washington, D.C.]], for the renovation of the [[White House]] under President [[Theodore Roosevelt]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Lumber for the White House |work=Madera Mercury |date=October 18, 1902}}</ref>

Completion of the [[First transcontinental railroad|transcontinental railroad]] in 1869 opened new markets for Sierra Nevada lumber, contributing to the expansion of the sugar-pine industry.<ref>{{cite report |last1=Litman |first1=Laurie |last2=Nakamura |first2=Gary |title=Forest History |series=Forest Stewardship Series |number=4 |publisher=University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources |year=2007 |page=4 |url=https://anrcatalog.ucanr.edu/pdf/8234.pdf}}</ref> Sugar-pine lumber production rose from about 35 million board feet that year to 349 million board feet in 1929. Production fell sharply during the [[Great Depression]], then recovered to a record 370 million board feet in 1941.<ref name="Betts1945">{{cite report |last=Betts |first=Harold S. |title=Sugar Pine |series=American Woods |publisher=United States Department of Agriculture, Forest Service |location=Washington, D.C. |date=July 1945 |pages=1–6 |url=https://archive.org/details/sugarpine1945bett}}</ref>

[[File:Sugar Pine Mill Flume Complex.jpg|thumb|Flume complex at the [[Madera Sugar Pine Company]] mill at [[Sugar Pine, California]], c. 1922. The company's flume carried lumber {{convert|54|mi|km}} to Madera.]]By the early 20th century, large logging operations had spread into increasingly remote parts of the Sierra Nevada, using logging railroads and flumes to move timber and lumber to mills.<ref name="LaudenslayerDarr1990">{{cite journal |last1=Laudenslayer |first1=William F. |last2=Darr |first2=Herman H. |title=Historical effects of logging on forests of the Cascade and Sierra Nevada ranges of California |journal=Transactions of the Western Section of the Wildlife Society |volume=26 |year=1990 |pages=12–23 |url=https://research.fs.usda.gov/treesearch/20500}}</ref> The [[Madera Sugar Pine Company]] and its predecessors logged forests in [[Madera County, California|Madera]] and [[Mariposa County, California|Mariposa]] counties until the company's own timber supply was largely exhausted by the mid-1920s, after production over the life of the operation approached 1.5 billion board feet.<ref name="LaudenslayerDarr1990"/> Logging also reached privately owned timberlands within [[Yosemite National Park]]. During the 1920s and 1930s, conservation efforts brought large tracts of sugar-pine forest under federal ownership and protected them from further logging.<ref name="GreeneYosemite">{{cite report |last=Greene |first=Linda Wedel |title=Yosemite: The Park and Its Resources: A History of the Discovery, Management, and Physical Development of Yosemite National Park, California |publisher=United States Department of the Interior, National Park Service |year=1987 |volume=2 |url=https://www.yosemite.ca.us/library/yosemite_resources/yosemite_resources.pdf}}</ref>

Sugar pine remained an important commercial timber after [[World War II]], but large, high-quality trees had become increasingly scarce after decades of selective logging. As mills began using smaller trees and a wider range of species, [[Abies concolor|white fir]], Douglas-fir, and other conifers made up a larger share of California's lumber production. Before 1942, sugar and ponderosa pine together accounted for more than 80 percent of the lumber cut by the state's pine industry; by 1956 their share had fallen to 52 percent.<ref>{{cite report |last=Baker |first=Harold L. |title=California's Timber Industries: Some Facts and Figures |publisher=United States Department of Agriculture, Forest Service |year=1959}}</ref>

Commercial harvesting continued at lower volumes in the 2010s. California harvested 112.9 million board feet of sugar pine in 2016, accounting for 7.2 percent of the state's timber harvest.<ref name="Marcille2020">{{cite report |last1=Marcille |first1=Kate C. |last2=Morgan |first2=Todd A. |last3=McIver |first3=Chelsea P. |last4=Christensen |first4=Glenn A. |title=California's Forest Products Industry and Timber Harvest, 2016 |publisher=United States Department of Agriculture, Forest Service |year=2020}}</ref>
